content.p: In the first week of December 1928, thousands of striking banana workers and their families crowded into the plaza at Ciénaga, a town in Colombia's Magdalena department. They had been told that the governor was coming to settle their dispute with the United Fruit Company. What arrived instead was a state of siege and a line of soldiers. The army opened fire. The event is remembered as the masacre de las bananeras.

How many people died is still argued. The official account counted nine bodies in the plaza. People in the banana zone insisted the soldiers killed hundreds. The United States embassy in Bogotá, passing on what company representatives told it, put the toll above a thousand, and one columnist writing in 2025 gives a figure near three thousand. No inquiry ever settled the question, and none of the pages consulted records a trial of those responsible. The officer in command, Cortés Vargas, was instead attacked in Congress, in the Liberal press and on the streets of Bogotá.

Banana growing in Magdalena had drawn tens of thousands of workers to the region. One Colombian columnist, Amylkar Acosta, estimates that between 25.000 and 30.000 workers were involved in the strike. Their complaints were ordinary and concrete. A worker, Aristides López Rojano, later recalled working from six in the morning until eleven and again from one until six, and said the labour contractor who paid the wages kept up to thirty percent for himself.

Accounts of the pay system agree on its centre. Workers were often hired through intermediaries rather than by the company itself, and their pay came as coupons that could be spent only in the company's own stores. Acosta lists the demands as better wages, an eight-hour day, and an end to those company stores. Colombian writers also describe a push for hospitals, compensation for workplace accidents and decent housing.

The University of Toronto's account dates the start of organised action precisely. On the evening of 5 October 1928, delegates of the banana workers met to discuss their grievances. One of them, Erasmo Coronel, spoke in favour of striking and the others agreed. At about five the next morning the workers handed the United Fruit Company a list of nine demands. Other writers date the strike itself from mid-November: Acosta says the union voted for a general strike on 11 November. The sources do not reconcile the two dates, which may describe a demand and a walkout rather than the same moment.

According to Acosta, the company refused to negotiate, saying it was under no obligation to do so. He describes it as a company that boasted of its power and was encouraged by the compliance of officials.

The government's answer was military. Acosta writes that President Miguel Abadía Méndez had issued a public-order measure called the Ley Heroica on 30 October, giving the state wide powers to repress protest. The ministers of government and war, Enrique Arrázola and Ignacio Rengifo, then named Carlos Cortés Vargas civil and military chief of the zone. The Toronto account says Cortés Vargas was appointed on the first day of the strike and was in Ciénaga with a battalion by the second. Acosta adds that public demonstrations were banned and a curfew was declared.

The United States followed events closely. US diplomatic telegrams collected by researcher Paul Wolf show the embassy in Bogotá reporting on 5 December that it had been following the strike through a United Fruit representative and through Colombia's foreign minister, who said the government would send more troops, arrest all the strike leaders and give "adequate protection to American interests". On 6 December the US consul at Santa Marta asked that an American warship be placed within calling distance, writing that the character of the strike had changed and that the disturbance had "a subversive tendency". On 8 December the State Department replied that it did not want to send a warship to Santa Marta.

The Toronto account says the workers learned on 5 December that the governor wanted them in Ciénaga to settle the strike, and they began arriving by the thousands. Acosta says they had gathered with their families since the day before to await a promised visit from Governor José María Núñez Roca, who never came. Just before midnight Cortés Vargas received a telegram carrying Decree Number 1, the official state of siege for the banana zone.

Cortés Vargas published his own version in a 1929 book, Los sucesos de las bananeras. The Toronto article quotes his account of the final minutes. He describes a warning to disperse, with a last minute allowed. "We had complied with the penal code," he wrote. "The last bugle call ripped through the air; the multitude seemed stuck in the ground." He then wrote that the order was given: "Open fire!!" Acosta adds that the drum roll and three bugle calls were followed by machine guns of the Schwarzlose type and Mauser rifles. Gabriel García Márquez later adapted the moment in One Hundred Years of Solitude, adding a word so that a voice from the crowd answers the soldiers directly.

Whether the shooting came late on 5 December or in the early hours of 6 December depends on the account. The Toronto article says the military fired "that night" on the workers and their families at the station. Acosta places it in the pre-dawn hours of 6 December. Trashumante and the Centro Nacional de Memoria Histórica give 6 December as the date, and El Universal's columnist writes of a killing on 5 and 6 December.

The toll is the most contested fact in the story. Acosta notes that people have spoken of thousands, of hundreds and, in the official version, of only nine, and that some have even called the massacre a historical myth. He says no one will ever know for sure.

The Toronto account describes the gap between memory and official record. People in the banana zone insisted the military killed hundreds that night, yet by official memory only nine bodies lay in the plaza. It quotes Josefa María, a supporter of the strike who worked out of Ciénaga, as saying the military deliberately left only nine bodies, "equal to the nine demands that the workers made". That is her interpretation; the article offers no other evidence that the number was chosen on purpose.

The US embassy kept its own tally, based on what others told it. On 7 December it reported that troops with orders "not to spare ammunition" had already killed and wounded about fifty strikers. On 29 December it relayed the statement of United Fruit's legal adviser in Bogotá that the army had killed between five hundred and six hundred strikers and lost one soldier. On 16 January 1929 it wrote that the company's Bogotá representative had told it the number of strikers killed "exceeded one thousand". El Universal's 2025 columnist puts it at three thousand or a number close to it, which is the highest figure on the pages consulted.

Many workers fled to the mountains, according to the Toronto article. Others stayed and, it says, tried to avenge their dead. Workers destroyed several company buildings, among them the engineers' quarters at Sevilla, where Erasmo Coronel was killed. The article says the company's archive at Harvard documents the damage to stores, living quarters, warehouses and telephone lines. It adds that of the five organisers photographed in a company portrait, one was killed, another jailed for fourteen years, and at least one other was targeted for death.

The American consul's account, sent on 11 December, was of looting and killing after martial law was announced and of American residents who held off a mob for six hours. By 9 December the consulate reported that a troop train had brought all American citizens out of the zone and that no Americans had been killed or wounded. The consulate added that guerrilla warfare was continuing in the zone and that the military was clearing the district of "the Communists".

In Bogotá, the Liberal press attacked the government. The embassy wrote on 11 December that it was calling the minister of war and the military "murderer" and "assassin", and that conservative newspapers were defending the government. The embassy added that, in its view, thinking people in the country realised it was the government's prompt action that had averted a disaster. Cortés Vargas defended himself by pointing to a report that two ships, supposed to be American warships, lay off Santa Marta. His report to Congress in July 1929 quoted a New York Times item in which Secretary of State Kellogg said he did not expect to ask the Navy to land marines. Cortés Vargas argued that the word "land" meant the marines were near and ready.
content.h2: Gaitán takes the case to Congress
content.p: The massacre might have faded had it not been revived in 1929. A historian writing in Trashumante says it returned to public view after the protests in Bogotá in June of that year, and after the speeches of the Liberal representative Jorge Eliécer Gaitán in September. By then Cortés Vargas was Bogotá's police commander, and the protesters carried placards saying "Venimos del Magdalena" and "Abajo Cortés Vargas". The US embassy noted skeletons and skulls decorated with bunches of bananas among the demonstrators' banners. The cartoons of Ricardo Rendón in El Tiempo kept the subject before readers.

Between 3 and 6 September 1929 Gaitán delivered what Colombia's Centro Nacional de Memoria Histórica now calls one of the most decisive debates in the country's history of labour and political violence, «Cuatro días de verdad». Its summary of the speech says he accused the army of taking orders from United Fruit employees, with troops quartered on company premises. He described bodies carried off in trucks to be thrown into the sea or buried in mass graves, and said witnesses spoke of people covered by earth while still alive. The summary says he presented bone fragments, including a child's, recovered in the area as evidence. He called it a "crimen sin nombre".

He also produced a telegram from the former war minister Rengifo to the United Fruit manager, asking for an impartial report before a state of siege was declared. He questioned the verbal war tribunals, whose verdicts, he said, rested on testimony bought or dictated by army officers. The strike's end, he said, was a deed fixing wages lower than before.

The US embassy recorded that Gaitán's attack was aimed mainly at the government, Cortés Vargas, Rengifo and Abadía Méndez, and that the company and even the United States came in for their share. In the translation it enclosed with its despatch, Gaitán mocked the claim about warships: Cortés Vargas, he said, "needed to seek an excuse for the unspeakable tragedy of which he is one of the authors". In his telling, the foreign threat was defeated by murdering people in Colombia.

The effect was political more than judicial. Acosta writes that Abadía Méndez's majority blocked Congress from naming a commission to investigate, and the matter was buried. The Trashumante article says the president paid a heavy political price for the events in Magdalena.
content.h2: A memory that outlived the government
content.p: The Trashumante study traces how the massacre was invoked in 1929, 1978 and 2008. In 1978, leftist parties and the national trade-union council organised the fiftieth anniversary. It produced plays, publications and public rallies, including one at Bogotá's bullring. Out of it came the monument at Ciénaga, Prometeo de la Libertad by Rodrigo Arenas Betancourt, which still stands and became a subject of debate in its own right. The speakers used the occasion to criticise the government of President Julio César Turbay Ayala and its security statute.

In 2008, the eightieth anniversary, people from across Colombia gathered in Ciénaga's central plaza. Those who planned the events linked the 1928 killings with the more recent case of Chiquita Brands, the corporation that succeeded United Fruit, which was accused of supporting right-wing armed groups that targeted union and peasant movements in Urabá. The academic volume Bananeras: Huelga y masacre 80 años came out of a conference at the Universidad Nacional in Bogotá.

The commemoration goes on. El Universal's December 2025 column says a gathering of unions and social groups, with Mintrabajo, was planned in Ciénaga for 6 December for the 97th anniversary, and notes a bill filed on 23 September 2025 by the labour minister to protect unions. In literature, García Márquez wove the strike and the killing into One Hundred Years of Solitude, as Acosta and El Universal's columnist both note. Revolución Obrera, a political publication, treats the massacre as a founding lesson for the working class, which is an ideological reading rather than a finding of fact.
